div.p: I have finished reading the book by R. M. Weaver Ideas have consequences (I could not do it quicker because of the regular time I felt I had to dedicate every day to the Systematic Theology).

I am deeply impressed by the fact that such a book should appear in this country under the auspices of the Chicago Press. This shows to me more than everything else the change of temper during the 14 years I am in America. Most of the criticism of our period given by the authors in the straight line of Burke (the writer of the most quoted book), Nietzsche, Spengler, George, Peguy and the group of Religious Socialists in Germany after the first world-war to which I myself belonged. Except the emphasis on the American scene and the references to the present world situation there is hardly a point of criticism which has not been made by those mentioned. From nominalism to pragmatism, a history of decay – – that is the common subject of this whole literature (compare Max Horkheimer's book Eclipse of Reason, (1947, Oxford University Press.)

Weaver's book, however, is more brilliantly written, more daring and radical than most of those with German background (except of course Nietzsche). I want to express my special thanks to the Chicago Press that it published and supports such a book which according to the still prevailing mood in this country is certainly highly popular. It will shock, and since the philosophical shock is the beginning of wisdom it will be very wholesome for the spoiled children in this country who are so excellently described by the author.

My criticism is, of course, directed against the last chapters which are supposed to give a statement of the positive elements left to us to build on them. Actually these chapters extend the criticism to many new points and do not give any indication of where to look for truth. When the author names private property as the last pillar, not yet broken, he adds that property in high capitalism which is merely a commodity you buy in order to sell, and often completely anonymous, is as much a distortion of the meaning of property as logical positivism is a distortion of the meaning of language.
In this he follows the criticism of Marx and the Religious Socialists but does not show a ground for reconstruction. It seems to me that he looks back – as the strongly criticized Romantics did – to the medieval synthesis of Christianity and ancient humanism. But he does not show how anything similar to that period can be born out of the ruins of the present world which he describes so excellently.
